lessons.good: Can I ask you a question?
lessons.why: Use the article “a” before a singular countable noun like “question.”
story: I was catching up with a friend after class.
We had a few minutes to talk before heading our separate ways.
I wanted to ask clearly without making the conversation feel like an interview.
When there was a natural pause, I asked, “Can I ask you a question?”
My friend answered and shared a little more about the situation.
I listened and asked a follow-up only when I needed to know more.
We found an easy next step that worked for both of us.
The conversation stayed relaxed and gave us what we needed to know.
I remembered the phrasing because it fit the moment so well.

lessons.bad: I wonder if you can help me with this.
lessons.good: I was wondering if you could help me with this.
lessons.why: The past progressive “I was wondering” is a conventional way to make a polite request. The present version is also grammatical, but can sound more direct.
story: I needed a colleague’s help checking one part of a report.
We were coordinating a small task with a colleague.
I wanted to ask for the information without sounding demanding.
I explained briefly why I was asking, then said, “I was wondering if you could help me with this.”
My colleague answered when they had a moment.
I thanked them and checked that I had understood the details.
That helped us agree on a practical next step.
The exchange stayed friendly and clear.
I used the same phrasing again the next time I needed to ask.

lessons.bad: Do you know where is the data stored?

lessons.why: In an embedded question after “Do you know,” use statement word order: “where the data is stored.”
story: I was trying to locate a dataset before starting an analysis.
Our research group was discussing a result during the weekly meeting.
I had a question that could help us understand the method more clearly.
After the speaker finished, I asked, “Do you know where the data is stored?”
They walked through the relevant detail and explained their reasoning.
I listened, then asked one follow-up about the evidence.
The group considered the answer before moving to the next point.
We left with a clearer picture of what the result showed.
I wrote down the question pattern to use in future discussions.
